passage: Monday: forty-two children, one slow fan, and the afternoon sun beating on the tin roof. By the maths period, Nikita Ma'am's class was shoving and squabbling; Charu snapped her pencil after a quarrel over desk space. Nikita raised her voice twice. It did not help. Wednesday: Nikita opened both windows, sent one group to work on the veranda, and gave a two-minute water break halfway through. The noise dropped. Friday: Charu herself reminded the class, 'Water break first, then fractions.' Nikita added one minute of silent sitting with eyes closed after lunch. The quarrel list on the board stayed empty all afternoon.

qa.q: How many children were in Nikita Ma'am's class?
qa.a: Forty-two children.

qa.q: What might Nikita have realised after raising her voice didn't help on Monday?
qa.a: She likely felt frustrated at first and then realised that the heat and crowding, not just bad behaviour, were making the children restless.

qa.q: Which of Nikita's changes seemed to help, and why?
qa.a: Opening the windows, spreading the children out and giving water breaks eased the heat and crowding, and the short silent minute gave them a quiet pause.

qa.q: How might Charu have experienced the Monday maths period?
qa.a: Charu was hot and squeezed for desk space, which led to a quarrel and a snapped pencil; by Friday she was the one reminding others about the water break.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing children grow louder and more quarrelsome in a hot, crowded room, and how fresh air, water breaks and quiet moments change their behaviour.

passage: Aadhya beti, you say your class is noisy? Listen to your Nana Asif. My first job, long ago, was in a village school: one room, sixty children and a roof that baked by noon. Every afternoon the pushing started. Bilal would kick the bench in front, somebody would cry, and I would bang the duster and shout 'Silence!' It worked for one minute. One day the headmistress watched, said nothing, and opened the back door and the shutters. A breeze came in. Next day I sent the children out in turns to drink from the matka and splash their faces. After lunch we sat quietly, listening to the crows. Bilal stopped kicking. I stopped shouting.

qa.q: What did the headmistress open?
qa.a: She opened the back door and the shutters.

qa.q: What was young Asif feeling when he banged the duster and shouted?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and helpless, because shouting worked for only one minute and the pushing kept coming back.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Asif's class, and why did it work?
qa.a: When the headmistress let the breeze in, Asif saw heat was part of the problem; water turns and a quiet sit after lunch calmed the children more than shouting.

qa.q: What might those afternoons have been like for Bilal before the changes?
qa.a: Squeezed into a baking room with sixty children, Bilal was probably hot and restless, which may be why Bilal kicked the bench; with breeze, water and quiet he settled.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, a teacher who sees children grow restless and quarrelsome in a hot, crowded room and learns that fresh air, water and quiet matter as much as rules.

passage: The power went off in the third period, and with it the only fan in Class 5C. Within ten minutes Vidya Ma'am could feel the room tilting: benches scraping, two boys fighting over a ruler, and Jaya, normally her neatest pupil, slumped on her arms snapping 'Leave me!' at her partner. Vidya's first urge was to raise her voice and threaten extra homework. Instead she opened every window, sent the monitors to fill bottles at the tap, and announced two minutes of silence with eyes closed. The room seemed to breathe out. Afterwards Jaya sat up and finished her sums.

qa.q: What did Vidya send the monitors to do?
qa.a: To fill bottles at the tap.

qa.q: What was Vidya tempted to do when the room grew loud, and how did she feel?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and was tempted to raise her voice and threaten extra homework.

qa.q: Why did open windows and a silence break work better than threats?
qa.a: The restlessness came from heat and stuffiness, so fresh air, water and quiet eased the children's bodies, and behaviour followed.

qa.q: How might Jaya have experienced the hot room?
qa.a: For Jaya the heat probably felt draining and irritating, so even her partner's small questions felt like too much.

grounding: A teacher sees children grow restless and quarrelsome in a hot room and restores calm with air, water and quiet.

passage: Yusuf Sir had learnt to read the afternoons. After lunch Class 6 came back from the dusty ground red-faced, and the room, built for thirty, held forty-six. Today a drill at the flats next door added to it. By two o'clock Preeti and her benchmate were shoving elbows, three boys were drumming on desks, and every question he asked got a groan. He did not reach for the punishment register. 'Bottles out. Everyone drink. Then heads down, and I'll read,' he said. He read a short story softly while the drill paused. When he stopped, Preeti moved her elbow back without being told.

qa.q: How many children did the room hold today?
qa.a: Forty-six, in a room built for thirty.

qa.q: What was Yusuf Sir feeling when he saw the shoving and drumming?
qa.a: He felt concerned but calm; he recognised that heat, crowding and the drill were fraying the class, not plain naughtiness.

qa.q: What small step could the school take to help afternoons like this?
qa.a: It could build in a water break and a quiet reading moment after lunch, so the class settles before new work.

qa.q: Why might Preeti act differently after the quiet reading?
qa.a: Once she had drunk water and rested, Preeti felt less crowded and cross, so she no longer needed to fight for bench space.

grounding: A teacher reads rising noise and quarrels in a crowded, hot room as a body problem and answers it with water and quiet.

passage:
'Ma'am, Gurpreet pushed me!'
'He took my spot first!'
Rashmi Ma'am looked round the rehearsal hall: sixty children, one door, the tin roof ticking in the heat. Voices were rising in every row.
'Gurpreet, come here. Your face is red as a tomato. When did you last drink water?'
'Morning, Ma'am.'
'And you, Manpreet?'
'Don't know.'
'Right. Everybody stop. Bottles. Line up at the cooler row by row, no running.'
'But Ma'am, the practice...'
'Practice can wait five minutes. Then we open the back door and sing sitting down.'
Later Gurpreet sang in the front row, his shoulders loose.

qa.q: When had Gurpreet last drunk water?
qa.a: In the morning.

qa.q: Why did Rashmi Ma'am decide to stop the practice?
qa.a: She felt concerned seeing red faces and rising voices in the hot, crowded hall, and wanted to deal with the heat before the quarrels grew.

qa.q: What worked here instead of scolding the pushing?
qa.a: Water, an open door and singing sitting down cooled everyone, and Gurpreet stopped shoving.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet have seen the rehearsal before the break?
qa.a: He probably felt hot, cramped and cross, so losing his spot felt like a big unfairness.

grounding: A teacher notices children quarrelling in a hot, packed hall and uses water and air rather than rules alone.

passage: Last April I learned something my training never taught me. I'm Yusuf, and I teach Class 4 in a corner room with one window and forty-two children. By the afternoon of the first hot week, the room smelled of sweat and chalk, and the children got louder every period. Lalit, usually my quietest, kicked a bench and shouted at his partner over an eraser. I kept adding rules, and my voice kept rising. Then I stopped and looked at them: red faces, droopy eyes, notebooks flapping as fans. I opened the door and window wide, sent them in pairs to the water tap, and read a story in a whisper with the lights off. Ten minutes later Lalit was lying on his arms, listening. Now we have a water break every period and a quiet story after lunch.

qa.q: How many children are in Yusuf's class?
qa.a: Forty-two children.

qa.q: How was Yusuf feeling as the rules and the voice kept rising?
qa.a: Yusuf was frustrated and tense, trying harder to control the class without seeing the cause.

qa.q: What changes calmed the class, and why?
qa.a: Fresh air, water breaks and a whispered story with the lights off, because the heat and crowding were driving the restlessness.

qa.q: What was the hot afternoon like for Lalit?
qa.a: Lalit was probably hot, tired and cranky, which is why even the quietest child kicked a bench over an eraser.

grounding: Shows a teacher seeing children grow louder and quarrelsome in a hot, crowded room, and fresh air, water and quiet moments working better than more rules.
